title: Stephen (Acts 6:8–7:60)
hook: the first to die for the faith forgives his killers as the stones fall
carry: lay not this sin to their charge

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beggar at the Beautiful Gate, walking and leaping. Your line was such as I have, give I thee. What did you give, when you had no cash? Day seventy-eight.
screen: `SUCH AS I HAVE, GIVE I THEE.`

segments.voice: Remember the argument about widows being left out of the daily food? The apostles solve it by choosing seven people to run the tables. The first name on the list is Stephen, a man, Acts says, full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. He's a food organizer. But he's also a speaker, and he gets into fierce debates in a Jerusalem synagogue, all of them Jews, arguing about Jesus, the temple and the law. It ends with Stephen hauled before the council, and people swear he's been speaking against the holy place. Everyone in the room turns to look at him. And Luke says they saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.
screen: `SEVEN TO RUN THE TABLES.` → `A FIERCE DEBATE.` → `THE FACE OF AN ANGEL.`

segments.voice: Stephen answers with the longest speech in Acts: the whole history of his people, from Abraham to Moses to the temple, told as a story of God showing up in unexpected places. By the end the room is furious. Stephen looks up and says he sees heaven opened, and Jesus standing at God's right hand. They cover their ears, drag him outside the city, and stone him. And while the stones fall, he prays two things. "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And then, kneeling, loudly: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." If those sound familiar, they should. On the cross, in Luke's Gospel, Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do," and then commits his spirit into his Father's hands. Luke tells Stephen's death as an echo of his teacher's. Now today's word. Martyr comes from the Greek martys, and it first meant simply a witness, someone who tells a court what they saw. Stephen is remembered as the first Christian martyr, and over the next centuries the word slowly changed, until it meant a witness who dies rather than take back what they saw. It's worth saying clearly: this was a bitter quarrel among Jews, since Stephen and every early believer was Jewish, and not a story about one people against another. And there's a quiet detail at the edge of the scene. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. Hold on to that name. Many churches keep Stephen's feast just after Christmas: December twenty-sixth in the West, the twenty-seventh in many Orthodox churches.
screen: `A HISTORY, TOLD TO THE COUNCIL.` · `LORD JESUS, RECEIVE MY SPIRIT.` · `MARTYS: A WITNESS.` · `COATS AT THE FEET OF SAUL.` · then, large: `LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one person in your heart. Sit, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who has hurt you. Not necessarily the biggest wound; one you can hold for two minutes. You don't have to tell them. You don't have to say it was fine. Stephen didn't say that. He asked that it not be held against them. See if you can let go of the charge for these two minutes, even a little. If you pray, you can use his words. If you don't, just loosen your grip. The bell holds the time.
Martyr. From the Greek martys, a witness. Stephen, the first, who forgave as he died.
Your line: lay not this sin to their charge. Today, when a grudge rises, try saying the line under your breath before anything else. Tomorrow, a chariot on a desert road. Day seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Christians honor Stephen as the first martyr, with a feast day on December 26 in Western churches and December 27 in many Orthodox churches. His dying prayer of forgiveness is often read alongside Jesus's words from the cross.

fork.setup: you're Stephen. the stones are falling. you have breath for one more sentence. what is it?
options: a curse on the ones throwing.
a final defense of your speech.
a prayer that this sin not be held against them.
fork.reveal: he kneels and cries out: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. then, Luke says, he fell asleep.

original.note: Greek: a witness, someone who testifies to what they saw. Later, one who dies for that witness.

trapdoor: what you thought: a martyr is someone who dies for a cause.
what it means: Stephen is a witness who won't unsay what he saw, and who forgives the people killing him.
what a scholar hears: martys was a courtroom word; Luke shapes Stephen's death to echo Jesus's, and slips in Saul, holding the coats, to set up the next turn of Acts.

notes: History framing: the script stresses that this was a dispute among Jews (Acts 6:9 names synagogue members from several places) and not one people against another. Confirm tone.
Luke 23:34 is missing from some early manuscripts; not mentioned in the script.
Feast days: December 26 (Western); December 27 in Orthodox churches on the Byzantine calendar. Confirm.
The development of martys from 'witness' to 'one who dies' is summarized as happening over the following centuries; confirm phrasing.
